speaker_label: MADELEINE BRAND, host
text: This is Day to Day.  I'm Madeleine Brand.

speaker_label: ALEX COHEN, host
text: And I'm Alex Cohen.  A while back on this program, writer Whitney Terrell introduced us to a soldier friend of ours, Captain Nate Rawlings.  Since then, we've been checking in with him from time to time.  Captain Rawlings is stationed near Sadr City on the outskirts of Baghdad.  He joined us recently by a pretty scratchy cell phone from his military base.

speaker_label: MADELEINE BRAND, host
text: Nate, this is your second tour in Iraq.  Last time, you were hunting down IEDs, improvised explosive devices.  This time around, what are you doing?

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (U.S. Soldier in Iraq)
text: This tour, I'm with soldiers that live with and train Iraqi army troops.  We're what's known as a military transitioning.  The Army calls this the mit for short.

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (U.S. Soldier in Iraq)
text: And mit teams across Iraq are partnered with Iraqi army soldiers. And we live with them, and then we accompany them on joint patrol and joint missions, where we're with them to provide air support, enablers, and also to observe their process, so that eventually, we can turn over inspections of Baghdad to their control.

speaker_label: MADELEINE BRAND, host
text: So you're training Iraqis to take over when you leave.  How are they doing?

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (U.S. Soldier in Iraq)
text: They're doing much better.  Last tour, we did a sort of disorganized version of this.  It was all that we could do to get them to shoot in the same direction.  And now, the entire battalion has a good staff process.  All those things that American soldiers take for granted as happening automatically is starting to come to fruition.  So wee really have seen some big improvements in the three months since I've been on the ground.

speaker_label: MADELEINE BRAND, host
text: So you think things are better now than they were last time you were there, in 2006?

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (U.S. Soldier in Iraq)
text: There's not even a comparison.  We were here when the Golden Mosque was bombed at the end of February in 2006, and it started the sectarian war, really, that raged for about a year and a half.  Whereas every other patrol we seemed to find a dead body in the streets from one sectarian conflict or another last tour, this tour, the people are starting to realize that sectarian violence isn't going to solve anything.

speaker_label: MADELEINE BRAND, host
text: Now, our listeners have been writing to you.  We have a special web feature where you take questions from them and answer them.  What kinds of questions are you getting?

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (U.S. Soldier in Iraq)
text: I've gotten a real variety of questions.  People have been asking what we do in our spare time. What food we eat, magazines we read.  And all the way to kind of heavy-hitting questions about policy for homosexuals in the military, overall motivation for the war from the Bush administration.  So the questions have been really interesting so far.

speaker_label: MADELEINE BRAND, host
text: What's your favorite?

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (U.S. Soldier in Iraq)
text: My favorite question so far might be what we read because I have a really diverse group of soldiers, and it was great to be able to talk about them.  And because they love all kinds of different books and movies and video games.  And in the future, for my future questions and answers, I'm going to try to write about my troops as much as I possibly can.

speaker_label: MADELEINE BRAND, host
text: So what do they read?  I'm curious now.

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (U.S. Soldier in Iraq)
text: As far as magazines, they read everything from Sports Illustrated to Esquire, Maxim magazine.  My mother's a librarian, so she sent me every kind of book imaginable from non-fiction.  I tend to read four or five things at the same time, so I'm reading a textbook on macroeconomics, "Last Exit to Brooklyn."

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (U.S. Soldier in Iraq)
text: My team sergeant has been reading "Seven Pillars of Wisdom," and then at the same time, he's reading a book by John Keegan about the history of military conflicts.  So we've got a pretty well-read and diverse guys.

speaker_label: MADELEINE BRAND, host
text: That's Captain Nate Rawlings.  He is stationed in Baghdad, and he will take your questions at our website, npr.org and answer them between his assignments out in the field.  So Captain Rawlings, thank you very much for joining us.

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (U.S. Soldier in Iraq)
text: Thank you for having me.

speaker_label: MADELEINE BRAND, host
text: From the studios of NPR West, this is Day to Day. I'm Madeleine Brand. Iraqi forces took control of Baghdad's Green Zone today. Iraq's leaders celebrated the moment, saying the country's sovereignty has been returned six years after U.S. forces invaded and toppled the regime of Saddam Hussein.

speaker_label: MADELEINE BRAND, host
text: Army Captain Nate Rawlings is here from Baghdad. He's with the First Brigade Combat Team of the 4th Infantry Division. He's a regular contributor to Day to Day. Happy New Year, Nate.

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (First Brigade Combat Team of the 4th Infantry Division, U.S. Army)
text: Happy New Year to you, Madeleine.

speaker_label: MADELEINE BRAND, host
text: Thank you. Well, so how do soldiers there in Iraq - how do they mark the new year?

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (First Brigade Combat Team of the 4th Infantry Division, U.S. Army)
text: Well, New Year's, like Christmas, is another workday for us. We've had our normal patrols and all of our normal missions going on. What we like to do, though, is to shift some of the administrative requirements from our day-to-day activities a little bit to later so that we can give the soldiers some time to rest and do the little things like watch a movie, play video games, just enjoy a little bit of time with their friends and platoon mates.

speaker_label: MADELEINE BRAND, host
text: And how do the Iraqis celebrate?

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (First Brigade Combat Team of the 4th Infantry Division, U.S. Army)
text: Well, a number of the Iraqis have wished us a happy new year. They know that New Year's is a pretty big deal for us. But right now, our new year is coinciding with the Ashura pilgrimage, which is a Shia holiday. And so, a number of the Iraqis are making their way down to the holy cities in Najaf and Karbala.

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (First Brigade Combat Team of the 4th Infantry Division, U.S. Army)
text: And the loudspeakers on a lot of the mosques are broadcasting prayers pretty much all day and all night. So that makes it a little bit interesting when we try to sleep, but we know that that's a real large holiday for them, as well.

speaker_label: MADELEINE BRAND, host
text: Right. So I don't know if you can characterize it, but what's the general mood there among the soldiers as the year turns?

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (First Brigade Combat Team of the 4th Infantry Division, U.S. Army)
text: Well, a lot of the soldiers are really looking back on this year as one where we've made tremendous progress. My unit in particular, when we left at the end of 2006, things were really rough, and there was a lot of sectarian violence. And we really didn't know which way this thing was going to turn.

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (First Brigade Combat Team of the 4th Infantry Division, U.S. Army)
text: And when we returned at the beginning of this year, in the beginning of 2008, we could really see that the sectarian violence was beginning to abate, and that's continued tremendously throughout this year. So we've been able to focus a lot of our efforts on stability operations and infrastructure and just helping with building up the government and the local government forces there. So it's been a really good, positive year, and I think that the soldiers all the way down to the lowest level can see that progress.

speaker_label: MADELEINE BRAND, host
text: And the Status of Forces Agreement, known as SOFA, went into effect today, and that among other things mandates the withdrawal of all U.S. troops from Iraq by 2011. Are people talking about that? And how is it affecting them?

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (First Brigade Combat Team of the 4th Infantry Division, U.S. Army)
text: Well, the SOFA basically states that we will be continuing to work with the Iraqi forces for the remainder of the time that we're here. And it has set a timeline, but our timeline to come home really hasn't changed even according to that. But a lot of the troops now are looking towards the future, knowing that they'll probably wind up going to Afghanistan.

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (First Brigade Combat Team of the 4th Infantry Division, U.S. Army)
text: So right now, the schedule of deployments, we don't really know how far out that's going to go, and so people are just sort of looking towards getting our job done here and then heading home to their families.

speaker_label: MADELEINE BRAND, host
text: And I've also read that most of the changes, at least initially, will take place at the Green Zone, where Iraqis will be in charge as of today.

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (First Brigade Combat Team of the 4th Infantry Division, U.S. Army)
text: I believe that's right. We're about five miles south of the Green Zone. And so for our operations, we continue to conduct our operations with the Iraqi security forces, and so not a lot has changed on our level there. But we'll continue to work closely with all the Iraqi forces in all of our operations throughout Baghdad.

speaker_label: MADELEINE BRAND, host
text: And, Nate, when are you coming home?

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (First Brigade Combat Team of the 4th Infantry Division, U.S. Army)
text: Well, right now, we're still on schedule for a 15-month rotation, but we're hoping to come home sometime this spring. And so, we'll find out in the next few months. As the unit that's supposed to replace us begins to get ready to come over, we'll start getting a little bit more of a date. But right now, we're hoping it'll be sometime this spring.

speaker_label: MADELEINE BRAND, host
text: And now, my producer tells me that you are - when you return, you're looking into going into possibly journalism. Is that true?

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (First Brigade Combat Team of the 4th Infantry Division, U.S. Army)
text: Absolutely. I've had a wonderful experience getting to really collect a lot of the thoughts from this experience and interview a lot of my fellow soldiers and officers and found that I really enjoy collecting those interviews and collecting everyone's thoughts for pieces and putting them down into writing, and so I'd love to be able to continue that.

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (First Brigade Combat Team of the 4th Infantry Division, U.S. Army)
text: And I think it's a really interesting time in journalism. It's a tough time right now because we're sort of moving from the idea of print journalism and subscriptions into a lot of online readership. But from what I've read, readership online and viewership online is really skyrocketing. So now, you can get those stories out to a much larger audience, which I think will be a great and beneficial aspect in the next couple decades.

speaker_label: MADELEINE BRAND, host
text: Yeah. Is there any area you want to focus on when you get back? Any particular subject matter?

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (First Brigade Combat Team of the 4th Infantry Division, U.S. Army)
text: Honestly, much to my mother's chagrin, I think I would like to come back to the Middle East and continue to cover a lot of the developments here, maybe Afghanistan, continue to cover a lot of our diplomatic efforts abroad.

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (First Brigade Combat Team of the 4th Infantry Division, U.S. Army)
text: I think that the next four to eight years of the Obama administration are going to be incredibly interesting, with a lot of the diplomatic efforts to just to try to put a lot of the things back together. Certainly, what's going on now in the Gaza Strip is incredibly interesting, as well. So I think, once I learn the business and learn a lot of skills, I'd love to go abroad as a foreign correspondent someday.

speaker_label: MADELEINE BRAND, host
text: Army Captain Nate Rawlings with the First Brigade Combat Team of the 4th Infantry Division joining us from Baghdad. And it's been great speaking with you. Have a great new year.

speaker_label: Captain NATE RAWLINGS (First Brigade Combat Team of the 4th Infantry Division, U.S. Army)
text: Thank you. Happy New Year to you, too.

speaker_label: MADELEINE BRAND, host
text: Nate regularly writes about his experiences at our website. You can read his latest essay on why some soldiers are getting nervous about coming home at npr.org/nate. And you can also send him questions about his experience. Again, that's npr.org/nate.
